text.p: Turkey is suffering from an "artificial" political crisis that warps the economy, retards foreign investment and distorts its credit ratings, a senior minister from the Islamist Welfare Party said on Wednesday.
Minister of state Abdullah Gul said Turkey's secularist media had fostered fear of the ruling Islamists and obscured the government's real economic achievements.
The result, he told Reuters in an interview, included higher domestic interest rates, hesitant foreign investment and expensive credit in overseas markets.
"If this artificial crisis we had last month, if we didn't have this, I am sure that now we would be in a better position," Gul said.
"Perhaps interest rates would have dropped to 70 percent," instead of their current level of about 95 percent.
Five weeks ago the military-dominated National Security Council directed the government to crackdown on what it said was the creeping Islamisation of Turkish public life.

The orders brought to a head simmering tensions between Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, who 10 months ago became modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, and the secularist establishment as embodied by the military brass.
It also prompted widespread speculation in the Turkish press that the armed forces were prepared to intervene for the fourth time in as many decades and depose Erbakan.
Gul downplayed any clash between Islamists and secularists over social policy but said investor fears were understandable -- if misplaced.
"In fact I don't blame the foreign investors. They are eager to come and invest, but unfortunately this artifical political crisis causes problems. Of course, they are right to hesitate.
"But I am sure they will understand this was artificial and they will come and invest here," he said.
Five international agencies have downgraded Turkey's credit rating in recent months, citing political uncertainty as well as fiscal problems.

Standard & Poors, for example, last month lowered the rating to B from B+ -- both sub-investment grades. Turkish banks have recently borrowed at stiff premiums of 70 to 100 basis points over London Interbank Offered Rate, or LIBOR.
The coalition government, nonetheless, remained united on the main direction of economic policy and was optimistic its record would win out in the end, Gul said.

This includes accelerating privatisation, spearheaded by court approval to sell off Turk Telekom, raising the retirement age to 55 to help stabilise creaking pension funds and coaxing lower rates and longer maturities from the domestic debt market.
"If another government did this, then it would have been appreciated," he said, adding the rating agencies would have to raise their assessments over time.
Gul said the Islamists had been undermined further by reports that they would undermine Turkey's relations to the international financial bodies and opposed free-market principles in general.
"When you look at the propaganda, we were against privatisation, we were against meetings with the IMF and the World Bank. This was just propaganda against us."

"We said we were not going to take orders. We are trying to convince them, but we are not saying, 'No, we are not listening to you.' We want to convince them and we want their support of course. I believe we will do this, we will succeed."
